title: SourceJS-LoRA: Source-Referenced Jensen-Shannon Divergence for Learning LoRA Merge Coefficients

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to expose why entropy-based coefficient learning fails for LoRA merging. Paper [12] analyzes the failure modes of entropy minimization, specifically why it works initially but fails after prolonged adaptation. It discusses overconfidence and model collapse, which aligns with the contribution's focus on entropy-based optimization leading to unstable coefficients. Paper [9] also highlights the limitations of entropy minimization, particularly its tendency to result in overconfidence and collapse, which is conceptually similar to the failure described in the contribution. Both papers establish the same empirical relationship between entropy minimization and failure modes, making the purpose covered.

### Mechanism
The contribution identifies that entropy minimization is reference-free, allowing optimization to drive confidently wrong predictions and unstable coefficients. Paper [3] introduces entropy-aware optimization, discussing how entropy dynamics can lead to overconfident predictions and poor calibration, which aligns with the mechanism described in the contribution. Paper [12] also discusses how entropy minimization drives overconfidence and collapse, which is equivalent to the mechanism of confidently wrong predictions. Paper [9] further elaborates on entropy minimization's limitations, including its tendency to result in extreme and unstable outcomes. These papers collectively cover the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates entropy-based coefficient learning by comparing its performance to uniform merging on GLUE. Paper [4] uses a similar evaluation design for LoRA merging, comparing different merging strategies and their performance on benchmarks. Paper [6] also evaluates LoRA merging methods using benchmark tasks to test skill composition. Both papers employ the same evaluation design — benchmarking merging strategies — even though the specific benchmark instance differs. Therefore, the evaluation is covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of merging task-specific LoRA adapters into a multi-task adapter. Paper [1] explicitly addresses merging multiple LoRA adapters for multi-task models, which is the same general application area. Paper [6] also focuses on merging LoRA modules for skill composition tasks, which falls within the same domain. Paper [8] discusses adaptive LoRA merging for domain incremental learning, which is another instance of the same general area. Thus, the domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: Learn LoRA merge coefficients without confidence collapse using only unlabeled data.**

The purpose is specifically to find merge coefficients for LoRA adapters that avoid confidence collapse, using unlabeled data. Paper [4] addresses "Model Merging with Unsupervised Expert Alignment" and trains merging coefficients without labeled data. Paper [10] (ZeroSiam) addresses "Test-Time Entropy Optimization without Collapse" — avoiding collapse during entropy-based optimization. Paper [12] (COME) addresses "Conservatively Minimizing Entropy" to avoid model collapse in TTA. However, none of these combine *both* sub-goals (LoRA merge coefficient learning + avoiding confidence collapse with unlabeled data) as a unified purpose. Paper [4] is closest — it learns merging coefficients in an unsupervised/unlabeled manner for model merging. The "without confidence collapse" aspect is addressed by papers [10], [12], [14] in TTA contexts. Paper [4] covers the merge-coefficient-learning-from-unlabeled-data objective most directly.

**MECHANISM: Minimizes Jensen-Shannon divergence between merged model's predictions and each task expert's predictions (teacher-anchored, source-referenced objective).**

The mechanism is JS divergence between a student (merged model) and multiple teacher (expert) distributions. Paper [16] uses "multi-objective divergence learning" for knowledge distillation, minimizing distribution differences between teacher and student. Paper [18] uses "confidence-aware multi-teacher knowledge distillation" with multiple teacher predictions. Paper [24] uses "balanced knowledge distillation" with MoE teachers. Paper [2] works on "functionality-oriented merging" using Fisher-Rao geometry to align predictive behaviors. The JS divergence specifically appears in papers [6] and [13], but as a measurement tool, not as a training objective for merging. The teacher-anchored distillation-style objective (student matches multiple teachers via divergence minimization) is covered by [16] and [18]. Paper [16] explicitly uses "a family of divergence measures" including JS divergence in a multi-teacher distillation setup. This is substantively equivalent — minimizing JS divergence between a merged/student model and expert/teacher predictions is the same primitive as multi-teacher divergence-based distillation.

**EVALUATION: Produces stable, balanced coefficients rather than extreme negative-weight values from entropy minimization.**

The evaluation design here is a comparison/ablation showing that the proposed method produces better-calibrated outputs (stable coefficients) versus a baseline (entropy minimization) that collapses. This is a controlled comparison/ablation design. Papers [10], [12], [14] all evaluate TTA methods by comparing against entropy minimization baselines and showing their method avoids collapse — same evaluation design (compare proposed method vs. entropy minimization baseline, measure collapse behavior). Paper [5] also deconstructs entropy minimization and evaluates collapse behavior. This evaluation design (proposed method vs. entropy minimization, measuring collapse/stability) is covered by [10] and [12].

**DOMAIN: Merging task-specific LoRA adapters into a multi-task adapter.**

Papers [1], [4], [8], [20] all work in the domain of model merging. Papers [1] and [4] specifically address LoRA merging. Paper [4] explicitly addresses "merging domain-specialized experts into a single model" with LoRA-based models. Paper [8] addresses "model merging" for combining individual models. This domain is clearly covered.
